name: Jacalteco
catalog_quote: Stress occurs obligatorily on the first syllable of most stems, on the syllable before a contour except in emphatic sentences and yes-no questions, and on a lexically determined syllable of some polysyllabic loans. (Day 1973:20)

audit.recode_to: contested initial~final: either keep initial (initial stress) downgraded from fixed-strict with contra + phrase-final caution (Tojolabal tojo1241 precedent in this catalog codes the phrase-medial/word-level initial pattern), or reclassify as final (final stress) per OKMA 2007:51 'palabras independientes se acentúan en la última sílaba'; owner's call after reading Day 1973 pp.20-24
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote check: the two quotations the record actually carries (DiCanio & Bennett preprint p.10; Day 1973:20 as relayed by the StressTyp2 entry for this language) are both present verbatim in copies we hold at the stated locators, and Bennett 2016 p.495 is confirmed too. The classification (initial, weight-blind, word domain with a phrase-final/pre-contour prominence noted separately and loanword exceptions) matches every source opened: StressTyp2 Initial, WALS 14A Initial/15A Fixed, and both Mayanist surveys ('normally on the first syllable of the word or root'). Nothing found suggests the classification is wrong, and the specialist literature as of 2016-2018 still cites only Day 1973 for Popti' stress, so no better stress description is known to exist — hence 'adequate' rather than 'at-risk'. It is not 'well-sourced' because the primary (Day 1973 p.20) has never been opened by us; the grade is quotation carried over second-hand from StressTyp2 via a database. Tw

sources.quote: "Phrasally-determined stress: Several languages in the Q'anjob'alan subgroup of Western Mayan have variable stress conditioned by phrasal position: stress is normally on the first syllable of the word or root, but shifts to the final syllable in phrase-final position. Phrasally-conditioned stress is well-documented for Q'anjob'al (5), and its close relatives Akatek and Popti' (Day 1973, England 2001)." (DiCanio & Bennett, Prosody in Mesoamerican Languages, preprint p. 10,)
